description:
verify's post-build cleanup can no longer restore the compose tree, so a
failed (or any) verify leaves /work/artifacts/compose/TARGET/ carrying the
verify-applied state instead of HEAD.

cli.py:394-410 documents the cleanup as three stages:

  1. make clean against the per-origin compose root
  2. substrate reset (load-bearing) - restore ports/ORIGIN/ to HEAD
  3. reapply against the now-reset substrate so
     /work/artifacts/compose/TARGET/ORIGIN/ reflects HEAD rather than the
     verify-applied state

Stage 2 was removed (cli.py:446-456). The stated reason: "Since B1 a verify
run gets its own worktree, destroyed with the job, so there is nothing to
undo."

That holds for the substrate and not for the compose tree. PORTS_DIR is
/work/DeltaPorts (layout.py:35), inside the per-job worktree and discarded
with it. DPORTS_COMPOSE_ROOT is /work/artifacts/compose/TARGET - env-level
shared state, outside the worktree. Destroying the worktree reverts the first
and leaves the second untouched.

So stage 3 now reapplies against a substrate that was never reset, and
re-derives the verify state rather than HEAD. The header comment still
describes the stage the code no longer has.

## Observed

2026-09-14, after the verify of lang_python314-20260912-021121Z failed:

    delta root   ports/lang/python314/overlay.dops   115 bytes, bootstrap only
    compose tree lang/python314/dragonfly/           6 patch files
    compose tree lang/python314/pkg-plist            5 PYTHON_PLATFORM, 0 _freebsd_

The compose tree claims six DragonFly patches that the overlay does not
produce. A dsynth run against that tree builds something the source cannot
explain.

Not additive residue: fsutils.py:132 copy_tree does rmtree + copytree and
plan_types.py:96 calls it on every incremental compose, so the output dir is
fully replaced each time. copytree preserves source mtimes, which is why the
composed Makefile still carries its upstream date while pkg-plist and
dragonfly/ carry the compose timestamp.

In this instance the cleanup also aborted early on the chained
`reapply MASTER && reapply SLAVE` (poly-lt5q.1), so stage 3 never ran at all.
But a clean run reproduces the same end state, so fixing poly-lt5q.1 does not
fix this.

## Scope

Not slave-specific. Any verify whose diff composes leaves the tree dirty; the
next build or operator inspection of the env starts from it. Same family as
poly-e56 (symlink not restored) and poly-451 (bootstrap written to the shared
checkout, composed in a worktree that lacks it): shared env state versus
per-job worktree.

## Options

- reset the substrate before stage 3, restoring what the removal dropped
- have stage 3 compose explicitly from baseline HEAD rather than from
  whatever the worktree holds
- make the compose root per-job so discarding the job discards the tree, and
  drop stage 3 entirely
notes:
Revisited against the code and the live env.

Confirmed in the env after the failed verify: /work/DeltaPorts -> ports-main,
ports-main on master, no worktrees left. Substrate clean, compose tree dirty -
exactly the split the bead describes.

Two things the first pass missed.

worker.reset_port already documents this defect on the agent side, in detail,
and cites poly-15l (closed, "The compose tree is regenerated on the wrong side
of the worktree reset"). poly-15l's resolution was compose-at-start in each
consumer, not a working cleanup. So build correctness does not rest on this:
verify's own build-stage reapply composes the worktree before dtest, and the
agent's dsynth_build refuses without a materialize_dports in the attempt. The
damage is a shared tree that contradicts the repository for anything reading
it outside the tooling.

Reinstating the substrate reset was not an option: its absence is pinned by
test_diff_path_runs_post_build_cleanup ("The source checkout does not: it goes
with the worktree").

## Implemented

dev-env/dports_dev_env/cli.py, _post_build_cleanup stage 2 now runs `compose
--delta-root /work/ports-main` directly instead of going through `reapply`,
which hardcodes --delta-root /work/DeltaPorts. Nothing is reset; the worktree
is left alone. Also per-origin rather than `reapply a && reapply b`, so one
origin that cannot compose no longer skips the rest - which is what let
poly-lt5q.1 take the whole cleanup down.

Tests: test_cleanup_composes_from_baseline_not_the_worktree,
test_cleanup_continues_past_a_sibling_that_cannot_compose,
test_cleanup_baseline_compose_failure_does_not_flip_ok. Suite 4016 passed.

## Left open

worker.reset_port stage 2 has the identical defect on the patch path and is
untouched here. poly-15l knowingly left it - its docstring says so - but it
fires after every patch job, not just verify, so it is the more frequent
source of a contradictory tree.
title: verify cleanup lost its substrate reset, so the compose tree keeps the verify-applied state

description:
Sibling verification and compose origin discovery were never reconciled, so
verify fails before it builds anything for every master port that has a slave.

poly-lt5q made two changes that work against each other:

- a slave's fix is authored on the master, so the slave keeps no overlay of
  its own (agent/steps.py patch_origin)
- the verdict must build the master and every slave, passed to the dev-env as
  `also` (verify_fix.py:171 sibling_origins_for, call site :314)

compose disagrees about what an origin is. compose_discovery.py:148
discover_overlay_contexts walks delta_root/ports/CATEGORY/PORT and only a
directory counts. compose_stages.py:524 then errors on any selected origin it
did not discover. A slave that correctly has no overlay directory is therefore
guaranteed to be rejected:

    E_COMPOSE_SELECTED_ORIGIN_NOT_FOUND

dev-env cli.py:333 chains the stage as `reapply MASTER && reapply SLAVE`
and cli.py:524 returns the moment it fails, so dsynth never runs.

## Observed

verify request 174, bundle lang_python314-20260912-021121Z, 2026-09-14T12:53:40Z:

    apply_exit=0  reapply_exit=2  dsynth_exit=null
    compose 1: ports=1 ops=11 applied=11 errors=0     (lang/python314)
    compose 2: ports=0 ops=0  applied=0  errors=1     (lang/python314t)

The fix under test builds green under the patch agent's own dsynth_build, but
cannot pass the verify gate, so it cannot reach accept. lang/python313 ->
lang/python313t will fail identically.

## Two smaller faults in the same path

The fail-open guards the wrong thing. sibling_origins_for returns [] when the
probe raises (docstring: "a probe failure must not turn a verifiable fix into
an unverifiable one"), but here the probe succeeds and yields an origin that
cannot be composed. The call site passes it straight through with no guard.

The post-build cleanup reapply in the finally (cli.py:463-475) fails for the
same reason and leaves the tree inconsistent: after the failed verify the
delta root carried a 115-byte bootstrap overlay for lang/python314 while the
composed tree still held all six dragonfly/ patch files.

## Options

- compose resolves a slave through its master (MASTERDIR), matching what
  patch_origin already does. Fixes the cause.
- move the fail-open from the probe to the use, so an uncomposable sibling
  degrades to a visibly partial verdict (master verified, sibling recorded as
  unverifiable with a reason) instead of failing the gate.
- whatever authors a master overlay also emits the bootstrap header for each
  sibling, so the directory always exists.

The bootstrap header is load-bearing and reads as scaffolding
("Step 48 bootstrap: deterministic header; patch authors the body"). Nothing
in its name says it is what registers an origin with compose.
title: verify cannot compose a slave port, so no master with a slave can pass the gate

acceptance_criteria: The rail scrolls inside itself with the page body still. The detail pane scrolls on its own. Selecting a row leaves the queue where it was, which is what poly-x3pg.6 was for. The test asserts the height constraint and not only the overflow property.
description:
Reported from a live instance 2026-09-13: clicking a queue row still throws you back to the top.

.repairs-split sets 'min-height: 100%'. min-height does not bound anything -- the split grows to its content, both columns grow with it, and '.repair-rail { overflow-y: auto }' never engages because the rail has no height to overflow. The element that actually scrolls is '.app > main' (min-height: 0; overflow: auto), and a full navigation resets it to 0.

So the split has only ever had ONE scroller, the page, since M4 shipped it. The detail pane does not scroll independently either; the two panes scroll together as one tall document.

This is why poly-x3pg.6's fix is inert. repairs-rail.js saves and restores .repair-rail's scrollTop faithfully, and that value is always 0.

WHY THE TEST DID NOT CATCH IT

test_each_half_scrolls_on_its_own asserts the split's CSS block contains 'overflow-y: auto' at least twice. It does. overflow-y with no height constraint is a no-op, and the test never looks for the constraint that gives it meaning.

FIX

.repairs-split needs 'height: 100%' and 'min-height: 0', and each column needs 'min-height: 0', so the grid is exactly as tall as the already-bounded main and each column can overflow inside it. The narrow breakpoint below 1100px already works, because there the rail gets an explicit 'max-height: 60vh' -- that path bounded it and the desktop path never did.
notes:
Fixed 2026-09-13, and MEASURED rather than reasoned about this time.

.repairs-split: min-height:100% -> height:100% + min-height:0, and min-height:0 on both columns (a grid item's default min-height is auto, which floors it at its content and re-breaks it one level down). The narrow breakpoint gets height:auto explicitly, because there the page should be the scroller and the rail is capped at 60vh instead.

Measured in a real browser at 1500x1000, through a probe served from /static so it was same-origin with /agentic and could read the iframe:

  BEFORE (implied by the CSS): rail never overflowed, main was the scroller.
  AFTER:  rail clientH=659 scrollH=4875 scrollable=true
          detail scrollable=false (its content was short)
          main   scrollable=false   <- the page no longer scrolls
          rail.scrollTop 0->600 landed at 600

Then the round trip poly-x3pg.6 was actually about: scrolled the rail to 900, clicked the 7th of 16 Ready-to-accept rows, and after the navigation rail.scrollTop=570 with the selected row present and fully visible. 570 rather than 900 because the selected row's group opens server-side, which shifts the rows above it, so ensureVisible re-centred it -- which is the designed behaviour.

test_each_half_scrolls_on_its_own now asserts the height constraint instead of counting 'overflow-y: auto'. The old assertion passed against a layout where both overflow rules were no-ops, which is how this survived M4 and a whole day of work on top of it.
title: The Repairs split has never had two scrollers: .repairs-split is min-height, so nothing bounds the rail

acceptance_criteria: Selecting an occurrence leaves the queue where it was. The group holding the selection renders open with no JS. The selected child row is marked. A deep link with no stored position scrolls the selection into view.
description:
The rail is its own scroll container (.repair-rail, overflow-y:auto) and every queue row is a plain link to ?occ=<bundle>. Selecting an occurrence is a full navigation, so the rail starts at scrollTop 0 again. At the 500-issue cap that is the whole queue of scrolling back, once per item -- which is exactly the case the split was built for.

Three things compound it:

- A multi-occurrence group's expansion lives only in the DOM (.wl-group.open, toggled by wlToggle). Selecting a child occurrence reloads, the group renders closed, and the row just chosen is display:none.
- .wl-child.current is emitted by the template and defined nowhere in progress.css, so a selected occurrence inside a group is unmarked even once the group is open.
- Every operator action in the right pane ends in location.reload(), so accepting a fix also throws the queue back to the top.
notes:
Implemented 2026-09-13. Three parts, because the scroll position alone would have restored you to a view of a collapsed group.

- dportsv3/tracker/static/repairs-rail.js (new). Restores .repair-rail's scrollTop from sessionStorage, but only when the page carries a selection -- arriving at /agentic from the nav is 'show me the queue' and starts at the top. Then pulls the .current row into view when the stored position does not already show it, which is also what makes a deep link land on its selection. Writes on pagehide rather than unload so it survives the back/forward cache and the location.reload() every operator action ends in.
- agentic_index.html. The group holding the selection renders 'open' from the server, so it is true with no JS. Groups opened by hand are keyed by data-issue and carried across the navigation by the rail script; the element id is positional (grp-<band>-<n>) and re-sorts as bands change, so it could not be that key.
- progress.css. .repair-rail .wl-child.current, which the template had been emitting all along with no rule behind it.

BEYOND THE BEAD: the chevron never carried aria-expanded. That was survivable while the group only opened on a click; now that it can arrive open it is the row contradicting itself, so the button gets aria-expanded server-side, wlToggle updates it, and the rail script sets it on the groups it restores.

Tests: five new in tests/test_repairs_split.py under 'the queue keeps your place', plus test_the_chevron_says_whether_its_group_is_open. _seed grew an 'i-twice' issue with two occurrences, because the sample had no multi-occurrence issue and therefore no group at all.
title: The Repairs queue loses your place on every selection

description:
Abandoning a job marks its row dead but leaves the .job file in
pending/, so the filesystem claim path picks it up again and the runner
works a job the DB says is retired. The in-process loop has no
cancellation check either, so once claimed it runs to its harness
budget regardless of state.

    POST /api/jobs/<id>/abandon  ->  state=dead, retire_reason=abandoned
    queue/pending/<id>.job       ->  still there, still claimable

MEASURED, run 293 (@2026Q3):

  16:16  operator abandons 3 queued java/openjdk25 patch jobs
  16:43  runner claims 20260912-155114Z-...-java_openjdk25-...-patch.job
         ("processing job"), whose row reads dead/abandoned
  20:02  still running: A1.T181, 1,460,191 billable tokens, in a
         4-flavor dsynth verification

3h18m of runner time on a retired job, and 57 other jobs sat queued
behind it the whole time. Only a runner restart stopped it.

Two defects, one visible symptom:

1. abandon does not remove the pending file, so the DB state and the
   filesystem claim token disagree. Whichever path claims first wins,
   and the file path does not consult the row.
2. the agent loop never re-checks job state, so a job retired while
   running keeps going to max_tool_turns / the harness attempt budget
   (observed: "attempt 2/8 ... 3265769/30000000"). Note this is the
   harness's own iterations/budget, not runner.max_patch_attempts.

Either one alone is survivable. Together, abandon is not a control:
it changes what the UI reports without changing what runs.

NOTE ON SCOPE

This surfaced because the pending files had been bridged from the
dev-env queue into the host queue to work around the chroot path
mismatch (the poly-b2r condition). Bridging is what re-armed the file
path. But the disagreement is latent in any deployment where the file
exists: abandon simply does not clean up after itself.

SHAPE OF A FIX

Remove (or move to failed/) the pending file inside the abandon
handler, in the same transaction that writes the row. Then give the
agent loop a cheap state re-check between turns - at minimum before
starting a dsynth_build, which is where the hours go - so a job
retired mid-flight stops at the next turn boundary instead of running
to budget.
title: Abandoning a job leaves its .job file claimable, so the runner re-claims and runs it to budget

description:
build_results is keyed by origin with no flavor column, so every flavor of
a port shares one row and the last write wins. Flavor results overwrite
each other: failures vanish and a still-building flavor reads as finished.

    dportsv3/db/schema.py, build_results:
        PRIMARY KEY (build_run_id, origin)

    dportsv3/tracker/db.py, record_result upsert:
        ON CONFLICT(build_run_id, origin) DO UPDATE SET
            version = excluded.version,
            result  = excluded.result,
            status  = excluded.status

port_status carries the same shape: PRIMARY KEY (target, origin).

MEASURED, build run 293 (@2026Q3, 100 operator-supplied origins):

UNDER-REPORTED FAILURES. dsynth logged 78 failures, the tracker 72.

    java/openjdk25        @jdk @jre @headless @jre_headless  4 failed -> 1 row
    x11-servers/xorg-server  @xorg @xvfb @xephyr @xnest      4 failed -> 1 row

6 results lost, and 78 - 6 = 72 exactly. The API agrees:
"failure_count":72 on /api/builds/293.

A PORT READS AS DONE WHILE IT IS STILL COMPILING. devel/llvm21 has two
flavors. @lite finished, @default is 2.5h into a compile:

    tracker:  - devel/llvm21 21.1.8_3 success
    reality:  325938 dsynth: [02] WORKER build devel/llvm21@default

@lite's success overwrote the 'building' status mark_port_building() had
set for @default. Same for llvm19 and llvm22.

"building_count":1 while dsynth had two workers busy, so the UI shows one
port building and the other is invisible. This is not a stale UI - the row
is wrong in the DB and refreshing cannot fix it.

WHY IT MATTERS

Failure counts drive what gets worked on. A port whose flavors disagree is
reported by whichever flavor finished last, so a green flavor can mask a
red sibling and the port is never queued for a fix. The inverse also
happens: a red flavor hides a green one and work is redone.

Distinct from poly-8dt, which is about dsynth recompiling flavors that were
already green. This one is about the tracker being unable to represent them
separately at all.

SHAPE OF A FIX

Add flavor to the key (build_run_id, origin, flavor) with '' for unflavored
ports, and to port_status (target, origin, flavor). Needs a migration plus a
pass over the readers that aggregate these tables - the *_count rollups in
tracker/db.py and tracker/progress_adapter.py - to decide whether a
flavored port rolls up as worst-of or is listed per flavor.
title: Tracker build_results is keyed by origin, so flavors overwrite each other and failures are lost

description:
The agent refuses every slave port outright, when the ports framework already
tells it exactly where the fix belongs.

`decision.py:294` short-circuits on `is_slave` to `escalate_manual` with reason
`slave_port_unsupported`, before the classification table. That rule is why
`security/krb5` and `databases/mysql84-client` were fixed by hand this cycle.
Its stated justification -- "inherits from master; no master-aware dops
support" -- overstates the gap. No new mechanism is needed. A master and its
slaves compile the same source tree, so a source patch belongs on the master,
and `DFLY_PATCHDIR` already points there.

## What the framework already provides

Mk/bsd.port.mk:1215 sets `SLAVE_PORT` and `MASTER_PORT` automatically from
`MASTERDIR`, and DeltaPorts' `DFLY_PATCHDIR?= ${PATCHDIR:H}/dragonfly`
(special/Mk/diffs/bsd.port.mk.diff:130) follows `PATCHDIR`, which defaults to
`${MASTERDIR}/files` (bsd.port.mk:1378).

Verified against the live @2026Q3 compose root for databases/mysql84-client:

    SLAVE_PORT     yes
    MASTER_PORT    databases/mysql84-server
    PATCHDIR       .../mysql84-client/../mysql84-server/files
    DFLY_PATCHDIR  .../mysql84-client/../mysql84-server/dragonfly

One `make -V` answers the whole question. security/krb5-122 is the worked
example: one overlay on the master, three ports green.

Some masters opt every slave into its own patch dir with the `${.CURDIR}`
idiom (e.g. lang/php82/Makefile:184 `PATCHDIR= ${.CURDIR}/files`), because
`.CURDIR` is evaluated wherever make runs. A static scan of freebsd-ports
main put roughly 29% of 1131 slaves in that group and the rest on the
master's dir -- but treat those numbers as indicative only, see below.

Both regimes work today. The agent only needs to know which one it is in --
which is the same `make -V`. Nothing in Mk or in the dops language needs to
change.

## Why the resolution has to be a probe, not a scan

The first pass at this resolved PATCHDIR by reading Makefiles statically and
predicted four broken overlays. Probing the live @2026Q3 compose root
contradicted two of them:

    devel/smake                       -> devel/schilybase/dragonfly   (dead)
    editors/pico-alpine               -> ./dragonfly                  (own)
    emulators/mupen64plus-video-z64   -> its own dragonfly            (own)
    multimedia/gstreamer1-plugins-bad -> its own dragonfly            (own)

Two reasons the scan was wrong, both structural:

  - it read freebsd-ports *main*, while the pipeline composes a quarterly
    branch. Ports differ between them -- multimedia/gstreamer1-plugins sets
    PATCHDIR one way on main and another on @2026Q3.
  - the composed tree is freebsd-ports *plus* DeltaPorts overlays, so no
    reading of either input alone predicts it.

`${PATCHDIR:H}` also degenerates in ways a lexical reader gets wrong:
editors/pico-alpine sets `PATCHDIR=` empty on purpose, so DFLY_PATCHDIR comes
back as the relative `./dragonfly`, which do-patch resolves against make's cwd
-- the port's own directory.

The conclusion is the design: ask the framework, against the composed tree,
per port. Only devel/smake is confirmed to ship a payload the build cannot
read.

## What is actually missing

1. The agent is never allowed to try (decision.py:294).

2. Blast radius is not covered on verify. A master overlay changes every
   slave, but worker.py:3270 `dsynth_build(env, origin)` is single-origin, and
   `dsynth test <master>` does not build the slaves -- separate origins,
   separate packages. So `rebuild_ok` on a master today means "the master
   builds", not "the fix did not break the siblings".

3. One existing overlay is authored on the slave when the patch can only be
   read from the master, so its payload never reaches the build:
   devel/smake's `dragonfly/patch-lib_getexecpath.c`, whose DFLY_PATCHDIR
   resolves to devel/schilybase/dragonfly. An overlay in the wrong place, not
   a mechanism defect.

   Moving it is a master change and therefore reaches every schily slave, so
   it wants the sibling build in section 4 rather than a blind move.

## Second hazard, unrelated to patches

engine/executors/mk_ops.py:35 `_mk_var_set_insert_line` inserts a *new* `mk
set` before the first Target or Include node; mk_ops.py:42
`_insert_before_last_include_line` (used by `mk eval`) inserts before the last
one. For a slave the trailing include is `.include "${MASTERDIR}/Makefile"`
(confirmed: databases/mysql84-client, www/yarn-node20; devel/smake uses
Makefile.master), so either way the op lands *before* the master is read. A
`mk set X` on a slave therefore survives only if the master uses `X?=` or
never sets X; a plain `X=` in the master silently clobbers it, and `mk add`
(`+=`) is worse. This applies only to variables the slave does not already
declare -- makefile_rewrite.py:44 `set_var` replaces an existing assignment in
place, and that case is safe.
design:
Works with the tree as it stands. No change to special/Mk/diffs/, no new dops
operation, no EXTRA_PATCH_TREE.

## 1. Resolve the relation instead of detecting slave-ness

worker.py:2138 `is_slave_port` greps `^MASTERDIR=` and answers a boolean. The
useful answer is the whole relation. Replace with a probe returning
`(slave_port, master_port, patchdir, dfly_patchdir)` from one

    cd "$DPORTS_COMPOSE_ROOT/<origin>"; make PORTSDIR="$DPORTS_COMPOSE_ROOT"
      WRKDIRPREFIX=/work/obj PACKAGE_BUILDING=yes BATCH=yes
      -V SLAVE_PORT -V MASTER_PORT -V PATCHDIR -V DFLY_PATCHDIR

cached per origin, with the existing grep as the fail-open fallback.
worker.py:2686 `_extracted_wrksrc` already establishes this exact incantation,
so it is a small function on an existing pattern. Verified working against the
live @2026Q3 compose root.

Derived fact the rest of this depends on: `patch_origin` -- the origin whose
dragonfly/ the build will actually read. The port itself when DFLY_PATCHDIR
resolves inside it, otherwise MASTER_PORT.

## 2. Widen the per-origin invariants to an origin set

Precondition for everything after it. Three invariants are scoped to
`ports/<origin>` and go quiet -- not red -- when work lands outside it:

  - worker.py:1973 `assert_port_clean` -- `rel = f"ports/{origin}"`. A
    master-origin change is invisible, so preflight reports clean while the
    master carries uncommitted work.
  - worker.py:1427 `_port_subtree_hash` -- the "substrate changed since the
    last successful materialize_dports" detector is per-origin, so a master
    edit does not invalidate the slave's baseline and dsynth_build can run
    against a stale composed tree.
  - worker.py:2551 `commit_port_changes` -- same `rel`; the triage-bootstrap
    to patch handoff commit misses a master-origin overlay and leaves it
    untracked into the patch job.

These are blind spots rather than gates, which is why they come first: a job
that writes at patch_origin would otherwise pass preflight and report green
with the change uncommitted or the compose stale, and nothing surfaces.

Note they are already reachable without this work -- the pipeline expects
fixes outside the bundle origin elsewhere (see "already absorbed" below), so
today the exposure is latent. This bead makes it load-bearing.

Take an origin set: the port, its patch_origin, and for verify the sibling
set. `reset_port` / `reapply <origin>` need the same widening so the master is
re-materialized.

## 3. Let the agent run, and point it at patch_origin

Remove the short-circuit at decision.py:294. A slave then classifies like any
other port. The constraint is not "which ports may be patched" but "where the
patch is written":

  - source patches (`file materialize dragonfly/...`, `patch apply`) go to
    `ports/<patch_origin>/overlay.dops`
  - `mk` ops stay on the failing origin's own Makefile, assertion-checked (5)

Coupling found on re-read: steps.py:440 gates `ensure_overlay_or_abort` on
`not is_slave` too, so no slave has ever had a header overlay bootstrapped.
Lifting the gate makes runner.py:3616 `_ensure_overlay_or_abort` ->
`probe_overlay_facts` -> `bootstrap_decision` run on slaves for the first
time, and it must bootstrap at `patch_origin`, not at the failing origin.
Cover that path before the gate comes off.

## 4. Verify the sibling set, not just the origin

A master overlay changes every slave. verify_fix.py:245 already replays the
whole changes.diff, so the master's change reaches the replay env -- but
verify_fix.py:191 runs `apply-and-build <env> <origin>` and worker.py:3270
`dsynth_build(env, origin)` builds one origin, and `dsynth test <master>` does
not reach the slaves (separate origins, separate packages).

  - compute the sibling set: every port whose MASTERDIR resolves to
    `patch_origin` (tree scan, cached per target -- 1131 slaves total, so the
    index is small)
  - build `patch_origin` plus its siblings before `rebuild_ok`
  - a sibling that was green before and fails after is a rejection of the fix,
    not a new failure to triage

The master/slave analogue of the flavour rebuild `_dsynth_run` already does
for meta-nodes.

## 5. Post-compose assertion

After applying an overlay, `make -V` the variables it set and confirm they
survived. Catches the mk-clobber hazard, and catches a patch written where the
build will not read it. engine/oracle.py already runs `bmake -V` per composed
port root with `_CI_PROBE_VARIABLES = ("PORTNAME","CATEGORIES","MAINTAINER")`;
extend that. Caveat: the oracle is best-effort and local -- it skips when
bmake is absent, so it cannot be the only gate.

## 6. Fix devel/smake

Probing @2026Q3 reduced the suspected four to one: devel/smake's
`dragonfly/patch-lib_getexecpath.c` needs to move to
`ports/devel/schilybase/dragonfly/`. The other three resolve to their own
directory and are fine as they stand.

NOT done as part of the implementation. schilybase has a dozen-odd slaves
(cdrtools, star, smake, sunpromake, schilyutils, tartest, ...), and moving a
patch into the master means it is applied to every one of them. That is
precisely the change section 4 exists to gate, so it should go through the
sibling build rather than be moved by hand on the strength of a probe.

## Blast radius: what the per-origin pipeline already absorbs

Audited. No gate blocks a cross-origin write today, and the two
architecturally hard pieces are done:

  - runner.py:4193 captures the diff whole-tree (`rel = "."`), and the comment
    names this exact case: "fixes that correctly land outside the bundle
    origin -- e.g. a slave port whose patch lives in the master's PATCHDIR --
    are captured instead of vanishing".
  - worker.py:2101: the whole-tree substrate reset was removed because each
    job's tree is a worktree destroyed with the job, so an escaped write
    cannot poison the next job. Its docstring names the slave/master case too.
  - worker.py:277 `_reject_orphan_dops_write` requires only the
    /work/DeltaPorts/ports/ prefix, not the job origin, so writing the
    master's overlay is already permitted.
  - verify_fix.py:245 replays the whole changes.diff, so master-origin changes
    reach the replay env.

Everything that does not absorb it is in sections 2 and 4.

## Acceptance

- databases/mysql84-client and security/krb5 reach auto_patch instead of
  escalate_manual, and their patches are authored at MASTER_PORT.
- `assert_port_clean` and `_port_subtree_hash` report a change made at
  patch_origin. Regression test: dirty the master, confirm the slave's
  preflight goes red and its materialize baseline invalidates.
- A fix on a master is rejected if it breaks a previously-green sibling.
- An `mk set` whose value the master clobbers is reported at compose time, not
  as a build failure.
- devel/smake's patch reaches the build, and the move is proved by a
  schilybase sibling build rather than asserted.
- `_ensure_overlay_or_abort` has slave coverage before the decision.py gate is
  removed.

## Explicitly out of scope

Changing DFLY_PATCHDIR, adding DFLY_OWN_PATCHDIR, or setting EXTRA_PATCH_TREE.
The 326 slaves whose master uses the ${.CURDIR} idiom already get a per-slave

description:
A full context ends the JOB. It should end the ATTEMPT, and the loop
should carry on to the iterations the tier already granted.

The remedy is already in the harness and the failure never reaches it.

WHAT HAPPENS NOW

tool_loop puts the request on the wire, the endpoint answers 400
"exceeds the available context size", and the exception climbs out of
attempt_loop into steps.py. llm.is_transient sees an unrecognized 4xx --

    if 400 <= status < 500: return False

-- so it is terminal, _err retires the job to failed/, and
_drop_bundle_branch_for_job throws the worktree away. ASSIST grants
max_iterations=8 and runner.max_tool_turns=400. One attempt is spent.
Seven are discarded without being tried.

MEASURED 2026-09-10, graphics/libavif, both on a local endpoint:

  qwen/qwen3.6-27b   turn 6: request 31,908 vs context 31,744 -> job dead
  openai/gpt-oss-20b turn 1: request 12,792 vs context  8,192 -> job dead

THE FIX IS ALREADY WRITTEN, JUST NOT REACHED

attempt_loop.py:417 -- every attempt after the first starts from a fresh
message list:

    if attempt_idx == 1:
        messages = list(base_messages)
    else:
        messages = list(base_messages) + [_failure_context_message(...)]

That is a hard context reset carrying a digest forward: the harness's own
compaction, at attempt granularity. An attempt that dies of a full context
is precisely the case it cures, and it is the one case that never gets
there, because the exception leaves the loop instead of ending the attempt.

FIX DIRECTION

Recognize context exhaustion where the request is made and end the ATTEMPT,
the way tool_loop.EnvironmentBlocked ends one today -- but continue the for
loop instead of returning. The next attempt rebuilds from base_messages and
has room again.

Detection: the message text is not standardized across providers, but the
shape is ("context", "exceed", "too many tokens", "maximum context"), and
LM Studio also returns a typed field, exceed_context_size_error with
n_prompt_tokens / n_ctx. Match on substring, and prefer the typed field
when present.

THE GUARD THAT MATTERS

If the FIRST turn of an attempt blows the window before any tool call, the
base payload itself does not fit, and every later attempt will fail
identically. That is genuinely terminal and must be reported as its own
thing -- "the payload does not fit this endpoint's context (N vs M)" --
rather than burning eight identical attempts and reporting a generic
give-up. gpt-oss above is exactly this case; qwen is not.

RELATION

poly-7eh reduces how fast the transcript grows. This bounds what happens
when it runs out anyway. They are independent: with 7eh fixed a full
context is rarer, and with this fixed it costs one attempt instead of the
whole job. Both matter more on a small window, which is the case that makes
a local endpoint -- free inference -- usable at all.

Also note free_tier=true sets the token budget to 0/unbounded, so on a local
endpoint max_iterations and max_tool_turns are the ONLY bounds left. Losing
seven eighths of the iterations to a recoverable condition is most of the
budget.
title: a full context ends the job, not the attempt, so 7 of 8 granted iterations are discarded

description:
_bare_model strips a leading "openai/" because "openai" is in
_ROUTING_PREFIXES. But "openai/" is a real NAMESPACE on third-party hosts,
not a routing prefix: LM Studio, Ollama and OpenRouter all serve ids like
"openai/gpt-oss-20b". The stripped id names a different thing.

MEASURED 2026-09-10, LM Studio on the LAN, graphics/libavif:

    _bare_model('openai/gpt-oss-20b', 'openai') -> 'gpt-oss-20b'

The endpoint had ONE instance loaded, "openai/gpt-oss-20b", at a 131,072
context. The harness put "gpt-oss-20b" on the wire. LM Studio does not
serve that id, so it JIT-loaded a SECOND instance under the bare name with
its default 8,192 context, and every request landed there:

    400 exceed_context_size_error: request (12,792 tokens) exceeds the
        available context size (8192), n_ctx: 8192

Side by side, same endpoint, same minute:
  curl  "model":"openai/gpt-oss-20b"  12,074 prompt tokens -> 200 OK
  agent  model=gpt-oss-20b (stripped) 12,792 prompt tokens -> 400

Unloading the stray instance by hand does not help: the next request
recreates it. Two jobs died this way and the cause was invisible from the
config, which correctly reads model = "openai/gpt-oss-20b".

WHY THIS IS WORSE THAN THE CASE THE CODE ALREADY GUARDS

_NAMESPACED_MODEL_IDS exists for exactly this, and says so:

    "meta" is here for the opposite reason to "nvidia": ... "meta/" IS a
    real namespace on somebody else's host (NIM serves "meta/llama-..."),
    and letting it become a routing prefix would strip half of those ids
    and 404 them.

"openai/" is now that case. It does not 404 -- it silently resolves to a
different model instance with different settings. A 404 is a bad name; this
is a wrong answer from a name that looks right.

NO CONFIG CAN AVOID IT

    return tail if head in _ROUTING_PREFIXES or head == provider else model

_ROUTING_PREFIXES is tested FIRST, so "openai/..." is stripped whatever
llm.<role>.provider says, including unset -- _provider_of infers "openai"
from the slash anyway. There is no setting that expresses "send the id
verbatim".

FIX DIRECTION

The signal that distinguishes the two cases is already present: an explicit
api_base. It means the operator has named the endpoint, so the model id
belongs to that endpoint's namespace and must not be rewritten. Stripping is
only ever right when we resolved the base ourselves from the provider name
(_PROVIDER_API_BASE).

  - Preferred: do not strip when api_base is set. _bare_model would need
    the base passed in, or the decision moves to the call site that already
    has both.
  - Narrower: add "openai" to _NAMESPACED_MODEL_IDS. Fixes this case,
    leaves "qwen/", "zai-org/", "mistralai/" on other hosts working by
    accident rather than by rule -- those already survive only because they
    are not in _ROUTING_PREFIXES.

Either way _use_openai_sdk must keep routing these to the SDK: the api_base
+ provider("openai") path is what makes a local endpoint work at all, and
that part is correct today.

TEST: assert the wire id for "openai/gpt-oss-20b" with an api_base set is
unchanged. Cheap, and it pins the distinction the docstring already draws.
title: _bare_model strips a real 'openai/' namespace, so a local endpoint silently serves a different model instance

description:
When tool_loop.run raises, the attempt's token spend is discarded. The
attempt is billed by the provider and recorded by nobody.

attempt_loop.run adds usage to total_usage on the line AFTER the call:

    response, attempt_usage, rebuild_ok_seen = tool_loop.run(...)
    ...
    total_usage.add(attempt_usage)

A raise skips it, and the exception propagates past api_call_complete
(the row that carries _usage_spend), so nothing reaches the audit.

EnvironmentBlocked already solves this — it carries `usage` and the
handler does total_usage.add(blocked.usage), with the comment "Without
this the caller loses the attempt's accounting and the audit
under-reports". That is precisely what every other exception does.

OBSERVED

www/chromium job 20260909-194249Z-2026Q3-www_chromium-309853-patch: an
attempt ran 13 h 41 m, drove a build to 34,886/54,854 targets, and died
on a 400. Its spend appears in no row, no patch_audit.json, no token
card. Three attempts on that port billed 13,139,714 tokens; the number
had to be reconstructed by hand from provider-side data.

This matters most exactly where the numbers are largest: a context-length
400 is the failure mode of an expensive attempt, so the attempts that
vanish from the accounting are the ones that cost the most. Any per-port
lifetime cost is therefore biased low by an unknown amount.

FIX DIRECTION

tool_loop already tracks `total` (it hands it to EnvironmentBlocked).
Make it reachable when any exception leaves the loop — attach it to the
raised exception the way EnvironmentBlocked does, or accumulate into a
caller-owned object (`messages` is already shared by reference, which is
what makes the poly-be6o session dump work).

Then in attempt_loop's `except Exception` (added by poly-be6o, which
dumps the session and re-raises): add the usage before re-raising, and
have the patch step log the spend on the api_error path.

RELATION

poly-be6o added the hook this needs — the except is already there, it
just has no usage to record.
title: an attempt that raises has its token spend discarded: the most expensive attempts are the ones missing from the accounting

description:
When harness_patch.run() raises, the patch step returns without capturing
anything, and the caller drops the bundle branch anyway. Everything the
agent did is destroyed.

OBSERVED — www/chromium, job 20260909-194249Z-2026Q3-www_chromium-309853-patch

  19:42:57  bundle_branch_checkout  bundle/www_chromium-20260909-193941Z (base=master)
  20:33-01:09  put_file x4: dragonfly/patch-third__party_perfetto_src_base_periodic__task.cc
               and dragonfly/patch-net_socket_udp__socket__posix.cc
  01:09:39  dsynth_build -> ran 8 h, reached 34,886/54,854 targets (63.6%)
  09:23:10  emit_diff relpath=overlay.dops diff_bytes=6923
  09:23:39  api_error 400 invalid_request_error
  09:23:42  moved job to failed/ ; bundle_branch_dropped (patch_failure)

13 h 41 m. Recovered afterwards: nothing. The bundle holds manual_handoff.md,
triage.md, triage_result.json and the TRIAGE session only. No changes.diff,
no patch session, no tool_trace. git reflog in /work/ports-main shows master
pulls only -- the agent never commits, so there was no commit to recover, and
the worktree that held the edits was destroyed.

THE TWO PLACES

1. steps.py:1277 -- the except does four things and returns:

     except Exception as exc:
         services.activity_log(... "api_error" ...)
         outcome = _err(str(exc), services, job_path, JobEvent.PATCH_GAVE_UP,
                        transient=llm.is_transient(...))
         if not outcome.detail.get("requeued"):
             _try_write_handoff(..., patch_result=None)
         return outcome

   Everything that persists work is below it, on the success path:
   write_patch_audit, write_tool_trace, the orphan reconcile, and
   write_changes_diff at :1349. None of it runs.

2. runner.py:4533 -- the caller drops the branch unconditionally:

     # Step 30 slice 4: patch is terminal for the bundle branch
     # -- delivery.diff was captured (slice 2) on success, and on
     # failure the branch's state is moot. Drop either way.

   "on failure the branch's state is moot" is the flawed premise. It
   conflates the agent trying and failing (state genuinely moot) with the
   harness raising mid-flight (state holds everything the agent did).

A THIRD CAPTURE POINT ALSO SITS DOWNSTREAM

session_dump is invoked from attempt_loop AFTER tool_loop.run() returns. The
400 came from inside the tool loop, so no transcript was written either --
which is why only the triage session is in the bundle. dump_attempt writes
straight to the artifact store (no local file), so there is no intermediate
copy to salvage.

THE TRANSIENT CASE IS WORSE

_err with transient=True returns status="failed" with requeued=True, so
success=False, so the branch is dropped just the same -- and the requeued job
restarts from master. A provider blip therefore discards hours of work
silently, and the operator sees a requeue rather than a loss.

WHY THE FIX IS CHEAP

_drop_bundle_branch_for_job runs at runner.py:4536, AFTER process_patch_job
returns. The except at steps.py:1277 is inside that call, so the worktree is
still intact at that moment.

And _write_changes_diff already does the right thing there: it diffs
whole-tree (rel=".") against the base via worker._git_diff_against_base ->
_git_in_ports_tree, which brackets the diff with `git add -N` and a trailing
`git reset`. Freshly-created, never-committed files surface as additions --
exactly the shape of the two dragonfly patches that were lost. emit_diff is
NOT the tool for this: it is a pure read that returns to the model and
persists nothing, which is why the 6,923 bytes evaporated.

FIX DIRECTION

- Call _write_changes_diff in the except at steps.py:1277, best-effort and
  wrapped so a capture failure cannot mask the original error. This alone
  would have saved the whole thing.
- Move session_dump into a finally in attempt_loop so the transcript
  survives a raise. Second line of defence: the put_file arguments alone
  allow reconstructing the patches.
- Consider writing tool_trace on the error path too; it is cheap and it is
  the record of what the agent actually did.
- Revisit "on failure the branch's state is moot" at runner.py:4533. At
  minimum, do not drop when the failure was a harness raise rather than an
  agent verdict.

RELATION

poly-3x8o and poly-9hjm are why the 400 happened: the payload floor was
~950k because 480k of never-read patches were inlined, and dsynth_log has no
byte cap, so the request carrying a chromium log tail crossed the provider's
ceiling. This bead is about durability and is independent of cause -- with
the context fixed, any provider hiccup at hour thirteen still throws the work
away today.
notes:
IMPLEMENTED (not yet committed) — all four fix directions, plus one hole
found while re-reviewing.

1. steps._rescue_work_on_raise, called from the api_error except BEFORE
   _err (which may requeue). Files three artifacts off one capture:
   analysis/tool_trace.jsonl (already in memory), analysis/changes.diff,
   and analysis/rescued/<job_id>.diff. Every step swallowed — it runs
   inside an except and must not replace the error the operator needs.

2. attempt_loop: an `except Exception` after the EnvironmentBlocked
   handler dumps the session and re-raises untouched, so a raise from
   inside tool_loop no longer leaves the bundle with the triage
   transcript only.

3. tool_trace is written on the error path (part of 1).

4. runner.process_job: the "on failure the branch's state is moot"
   comment is replaced. The DROP ITSELF IS UNCHANGED, deliberately —
   the worktree is keyed on bundle_id, so keeping a dirty one makes the
   requeued job hard-refuse at assert_port_clean, turning a recoverable
   provider blip into a permanent refusal. The bead's suggestion to
   keep the branch on a harness raise would have made things worse. The
   capture moving inside the step is what makes dropping safe, and the
   comment now says so.

THE HOLE THE BEAD DID NOT NAME

Writing only to changes.diff is not durable. A requeued attempt that
gives up cleanly writes its own diff over it — and that diff is empty,
because the retry starts from base and the rescued edits are not in its
tree. So the rescue would have been undone by the retry it enabled.
Hence analysis/rescued/<job_id>.diff, which no later job overwrites.
Same convention as the session dumps; shows in the UI under "Other".

TWO SUPPORTING CHANGES TO _write_changes_diff

- only_if_nonempty: skip the write when the capture is empty, and RAISE
  on a capture failure rather than filing a tombstone. On the rescue
  path "nothing to save" and "could not look" are different answers and
  the caller reports them differently (patch_work_rescue_empty vs
  patch_work_rescue_failed).
- rc != 0 is now a failed capture, not an empty one. Previously an
  unreachable chroot produced empty stdout, which every reader
  downstream reads as "the agent changed nothing" — the one answer
  indistinguishable from a real loss. Default path still files a
  tombstone, now naming the git error.

EMERGENT: _try_write_handoff runs after the rescue and reads
changes.diff, so manual_handoff.md now summarizes the rescued work
instead of being silent. Pinned by a test.

20 tests in tests/test_patch_raise_rescue.py. Suite 3,868 passed.

NOT FIXED HERE: the attempt's token spend is still discarded on the
raise path — filed as poly-cg6u.1 under the token-economy epic.
title: a harness raise loses everything the patch agent did: no changes.diff, no session, and the branch is dropped anyway

description:
dsynth supports a compiler cache and the dev-env writes it off:

  dev-env/dports_dev_env/dsynth.py:53
      Directory_ccache= disabled

Every agent build round therefore recompiles the port from zero. On
www/firefox that is the ~45 min poly-7ska measures. On www/chromium it is
about thirteen hours.

MEASURED — www/chromium, the attempt running 2026-09-10

  dsynth_build started            01:09:39 UTC
  at 08:11:44                     34,337 / 54,854 targets  (62.6%)
  at 08:21:07                     34,886 / 54,854          (63.6%)
  spot rate                       58.5 targets/min
  projected finish                ~14:00-14:30 UTC, i.e. ~13 h

Rate curve from 28,764 object mtimes: 138/min early on cheap targets,
down to 17/min around 06:00, recovered to 45-59/min in Blink's V8
bindings. The tail is link-heavy, so the last percent crawls.

The agent's loop is edit-one-patch -> rebuild. Those edits touch one or two
leaf .cc files. With a warm cache the other ~54,000 objects hit and the
round should fall to tens of minutes; without one, every round is the whole
thirteen hours. That is the difference between a port that can be iterated
and one that gets a single attempt a day.

WHERE THE CHANGE GOES

Four places, all in the dev-env distribution:

1. dev-env/dports_dev_env/config.py — one Setting entry in the dev_env
   table, next to dsynth_builders / dsynth_jobs. Per CLAUDE.md every
   configurable value is one entry there and no environment variable.
   Something like dev_env.dsynth_ccache (bool, default False) or a path.

2. dev-env/dports_dev_env/config.py — matching typed field on DevEnvConfig
   (dataclass at line ~31-38) and its construction at ~184-193.

3. dev-env/dports_dev_env/dsynth.py — write_dsynth_config():
   - add dsynth_root / "ccache" to the mkdir list (lines 30-37)
   - emit Directory_ccache= /work/dsynth/ccache instead of "disabled"
   The path must be the in-chroot one, like every other Directory_ entry.

4. dev-env/dports_dev_env/config.py — dev_env.tool_pkgs_optional, which is
   how the env provisions tooling. ccache is NOT installed on the builder
   today: `pkg info -x ccache` -> "No package(s) matching ccache". dsynth
   only wires the directory; the ports framework still needs the binary
   present in the worker jail.

Editing the live /usr/local/etc/... dsynth.ini instead would be reverted by
the next env refresh, since dsynth.py regenerates it.

SPACE

/     303G, 241G free
/build 101G,  71G free
existing dsynth tree 43G

Chromium's cache is plausibly 15-30G. Not a constraint here.

CAVEATS

- dsynth reads its config at startup, so this cannot help a build already
  running, and the env refresh should wait until one finishes.
- The first build after enabling is a cold cache and saves nothing. The
  payoff starts on the round after that.
- chromium compiles with -fprofile-use=<...>.profdata; ccache has to hash
  that input. Worth confirming the hit rate on the second build rather than
  assuming it.
- A patch to a widely-included header still invalidates a large slice. Leaf
  .cc patches, which is what portability fixes usually are, should hit.

RELATION TO poly-7ska

Same goal, different mechanism, and they compose. poly-7ska keeps the
objdir and mounts alive (dsynth debug) so an incremental gmake is possible;
it changes how the agent drives a build. ccache leaves dsynth's
force-rebuild exactly as it is and makes the recompile cheap instead,
surviving the jail teardown that poly-7ska works around. ccache is the
smaller change: configuration plus a package, no tool-loop work.
title: dev-env writes Directory_ccache= disabled, so every agent build round recompiles from zero — 13 hours on chromium

  1            92   2,242,243        3%    3                  1,959,653  87%
  2            58   5,365,245        1%    8                  5,255,552  98%
  3           154   5,532,226        2%    6                  4,645,529  84%
                   ----------                                 ---------
                   13,139,714                                 ~11.9M

Model output is 1-3% of spend. Everything else is re-sent input, and a
re-send costs 620-840k because the payload is that big. 17 misses did it.

Cache behaviour itself does not look controllable from here: misses follow
gaps as short as 33s and hits as long as 173s, after every kind of tool, so
it is not a TTL and not tied to the ~5 min dsynth_build. Payload size is the
part we own.

THE PER-FILE CAP DOES NOT HELP

runner.context_file_cap = 32768. Across the 1,604 subsections: median 780
chars, mean 1,198, max 26,376. Zero were truncated. The cap was added for
the opposite shape -- PortFilesSection's docstring cites python311's 533 KB
pkg-plist -- and a per-file cap cannot see 1,604 individually-reasonable
files. There is no section-level or payload-level budget.

THE SELECTION IS ALSO WRONG

context.py:472 filters on p.startswith("port/files/patch-"). For chromium:

  composed files/       1606 (1604 patch-*, plus chrome.in, chromium-browser.desktop.in)
  composed dragonfly/    144
  in both                 96   ours overriding a FreeBSD patch of the same name
  dragonfly-only          48
  bundle port/dragonfly/   0

So the agent is shipped 1,604 FreeBSD patches and none of the overlay's own.
Spot-checked four dragonfly-only patches (patch-base_process_launch__posix.cc
and three others): none appear in the payload. For the 96 shared names it
sees the FreeBSD content, not the DragonFly override that the port actually
carries. A patch agent working on a DragonFly overlay is being shown
everything except the DragonFly patches.

WHAT THE AGENT ACTUALLY USED

Same session, its own retrieval across 92 turns:

  get_file               14 calls    ~14,772 tok
  grep                   15 calls    ~19,504 tok
  get_effective_overlay   1 call      ~4,109 tok
  dops_reference          1 call      ~3,088 tok
  list_dir                2 calls       ~402 tok
  TOTAL                  33 calls    ~41,876 tok

It has the tools and uses them. Fetching on demand costs ~42k against
~480k for inlining everything up front.

FIX DIRECTION

- Give the section a total budget, not just a per-file one, and prefer a
  manifest over bodies past that budget: 1,604 filenames is ~50k chars
  (~12k tok) against ~480k for the contents.
- Include the overlay's dragonfly/ patches, and where a name exists in both,
  show the one that governs.
- Consider ordering by relevance to the failing build rather than sorted()
  when a budget forces a choice.

Payload would drop ~514k -> ~35k, making every cache miss ~15x cheaper. The
same three attempts fit inside the old 5M tier budget with room to spare.
Note this also bounds the value of raising policy.tiers.ASSIST.max_tokens to
30M (done 2026-09-09): at 800k a miss that mostly buys more expensive misses.

CORRECTION TO AN EARLIER READING

Splitting www/chromium's monolithic dragonfly/patch-all into 142 per-file
patches (2026-09-09) did NOT contribute. Those live in dragonfly/, which the
payload does not include. The 1,604 are FreeBSD's own and predate it.
design:
REVISED after looking at what other harnesses do. The first draft proposed
"budget + rank + inline until the budget is spent". That is still the wrong
shape. No comparable harness pushes file bodies into the prompt at all.

WHY runner.context_file_cap IS THE WRONG PRIMITIVE

It is used in exactly one place -- context.py -- i.e. only on content pushed
into the prompt unasked. The pull side already does the right thing:
get_file takes limit_lines plus start_line/end_line, which is ordinary
pagination.

A per-file cap on pushed content fails twice over:
  - it cannot bound the total. 1,604 files x median 780 chars = 480k tokens,
    every one of them under the 32,768 cap, zero truncated.
  - when it does fire it hands the model a head+tail splice of a file it
    never asked for, with no way to know what was elided.

PRIOR ART

Aider (aider.chat/2023/10/22/repomap.html) does not inline files. It builds a
repo MAP: a graph of symbol definitions and references, personalized PageRank
to rank by relevance, then renders top-ranked DEFINITIONS -- signatures, not
bodies -- binary-searched to fit a token budget that defaults to 1k tokens.
We spend 480k on the same job.

SWE-agent (arxiv.org/abs/2405.15793) rejects inlining explicitly: "Flooding a
language agent's context window with too much file content can be
inefficient, since the majority of file content is usually irrelevant to the
issue," and notes such inefficiency "can exhaust an agent's cost budget or
context window, leading to even worse performance." It gives the agent
windowed viewing (100-line windows) with scroll/goto instead.

Claude Code, Pi and OpenClaw cap file READS -- 256KB stat check, 2,000 lines
or 50KB -- and pair the cap with offset/limit pagination, persisting
oversized results outside the context. The cap belongs on what a tool
returns when asked, which is where ours already is for get_file.

On truncation as such: "Truncation that's too aggressive isn't just lossy --
it's misleadingly lossy, because the agent has no way to know it's missing
the relevant span."

REVISED FIX

1. ExistingPatchesSection emits a MANIFEST, not bodies. Names only, grouped,
   with the dragonfly/ override marked where a basename exists in both. For
   chromium that is ~1,604 names (~50k chars) or, better, per-directory
   counts plus the paths -- against 1,921,730 chars today.

2. No inlined bodies by default. The measured case for inlining is empty:
   in attempt 1 the agent made 14 get_file calls and read NONE of the 1,604
   patches. It read overlay.dops, the port Makefile, Mk/Features/lto.mk,
   bootstrap.py, gen.py, libcxx22/newport/Makefile -- several with
   start_line/end_line. It fetches precisely when it wants something.

3. Name the location. The manifest should give the composed port path
   (/work/artifacts/compose/@2026Q3/<origin>/files and .../dragonfly) so
   get_file and list_dir reach the real files. The agent already reads live
   chroot paths, so it needs no bundle artifact to see a patch.

4. Leave runner.context_file_cap alone for PULLED results, and stop using it
   as if it were a section budget. If a pushed section ever needs a bound,
   it needs a section-level budget, not a per-file one -- but per 2, the
   right bound here is zero bodies.

5. Optional, later: if orientation beyond names proves useful, the Aider
   shape is the model -- rank by relevance to the failing build (patches
   whose target path appears in logs/errors.txt), and render something
   smaller than a body, e.g. the ---/+++ header and hunk count.

WHAT DOES NOT CHANGE

Layer 1 stands: hook_pkg_failure has no dragonfly/ loop, so no bundle has
port/dragonfly/ artifacts and the overlay's own patches are invisible. That
is a correctness bug independent of the token question, and a manifest that
lists only port/files/ would still be wrong.

EXPECTED EFFECT

Payload 514k -> ~35k plus a names list. Cache misses ~15x cheaper. The three
attempts that cost 13.1M fit inside the old 5M tier budget. And per
SWE-agent's finding, less irrelevant content should improve the agent's
behaviour, not merely its cost.
title: the patch payload inlines every port/files patch — 93% of chromium's prompt, and it omits the overlay's own dragonfly patches

description:
The proof-block orphan rescue in attempt_loop cannot tell "no proof block
emitted" from "proof block emitted saying false", so it overrides an explicit
gave-up report and resolves the bundle agent_fixed.

OBSERVED

www_chromium-20260909-135208Z, patch attempt 1. The agent's own analysis/patch.md:

  ## Rebuild Status
  gave-up

  ## Rebuild Proof (JSON)
  { "rebuild_ok": false }

and in its summary: "the link then fails on undefined reference to
'__cxa_thread_atexit' ... which I could not resolve within this attempt".

The agent was correct and honest. What got written was
analysis/rebuild_proof.json:

  { "rebuild_ok": true, "source": "tool_result", ... }

and the bundle resolved resolution=agent_fixed on a port whose last
dsynth_build returned rebuild_ok=False.

MECHANISM

attempt_loop.py:592-612

    proof = _parse(prev_text)
    rebuild_ok = bool(_ok(proof))
    ...
    if not rebuild_ok and rebuild_ok_seen and is_success is None:
        proof = {"rebuild_ok": True, "source": "tool_result"}
        rebuild_ok = True

Two problems.

1. `not rebuild_ok` is satisfied by BOTH an absent proof block and a proof
   block that explicitly says false. The comment above the branch only
   contemplates the first ("the LLM may have run out of budget before it
   could emit ## Rebuild Proof (JSON)"). Nothing distinguishes them, so an
   explicit negative is silently upgraded.

2. `is_success is None` reads like a status guard but is not one. It is the
   optional custom success-predicate parameter, None for every patch run
   (convert passes its own). It never blocks anything here.

`rebuild_ok_seen` is also sticky for the whole attempt. Here it was set at
14:22:40 by a dsynth_build that returned rebuild_ok=True after 4 seconds --
against ~5 minutes for the real builds in the same attempt -- then survived
four subsequent FAIL builds over the next 30 minutes to arm the rescue at
14:54:43. Even a rescue that only fired on a genuinely absent proof would be
lifting a stale True.

RELATION TO poly-qkp

Same rescue, same synthesized {"rebuild_ok": true, "source": "tool_result"},
same bogus agent_fixed. poly-qkp is the attempt hitting the turn cap so no
final report exists -- the case the branch was written for. This is the
branch firing against a report that exists and says gave-up. A fix that only
addresses the turn-cap path leaves this one open, and vice versa; most
likely both want the same repair.

FIX DIRECTION

- Distinguish absent proof from negative proof. Only rescue when _parse
  returned nothing at all; never when it returned rebuild_ok=false.
- Do not lift a stale rebuild_ok_seen. If the rescue is kept, gate it on the
  MOST RECENT dsynth_build result, not on any-time-during-the-attempt.
- Rename or remove the `is_success is None` clause; it does not do what it
  reads as.

SECONDARY, NOT VERIFIED

Why the 14:22:40 build exited 0 in 4 seconds is unconfirmed. rebuild_ok is
p.returncode == 0 (worker.py:3264, identical in the installed copy on the
builder) with no guard for dsynth ignoring or skipping a port rather than
compiling it, and tools.py:169 asserts to the model that "rebuild_ok=true
means rc==0, i.e. it built AND passed the gate". The ignore/skip hypothesis
has NOT been tested; the per-port log was overwritten by later attempts and
agent builds run hooks-disabled, so nothing was recorded. Confirm before
acting.
title: the proof-block orphan rescue overrides an explicit rebuild_ok:false, so a gave-up attempt still reports agent_fixed

description:
A `type dport` port can never be classified `converted`, so the patch flow
escalates every successful fix on one. Affects 88 ports.

WHAT HAPPENED (devel/libcxx22, 2026-09-08)

  bundle devel_libcxx22-20260908-224530Z
  patch job 20260908-225449Z-2026Q3-devel_libcxx22-554173-patch.job

check-plist failed (577 `Error: Orphaned:` + 1 `Error: Missing:`). The agent
edited `ports/devel/libcxx22/newport/pkg-plist` -- the correct and only
surface for a dport -- adding exactly the 577 orphans and removing the 1
missing entry. Rebuild passed: rebuild_ok=True, patch status=success.

It was then escalated:

  Reason: patch_non_dops_substrate
  Detail: build passed but port dops_state='needs_judgment'
          (expected 'converted'); fix likely written as compat artifacts
          instead of overlay.dops

That detail is false. There are no compat artifacts; the agent edited the
only file that exists. Cost: 963,612 billable over 213 turns, discarded.

MECHANISM

The gate is steps.py:1415:

    post_state = ctx.state.get("post_patch_dops_state")
    if post_state != "converted":
        ... ESCALATE_MANUAL, reason="patch_non_dops_substrate"

Correct for a `type port`: a build that went green by editing a leftover
Makefile.DragonFly is not a dops fix and should not be stamped agent_fixed.

`post_patch_dops_state` comes from classify_dops -> assess_overlay
(overlay_state.py). There, `newport/` is counted as an unmigrated legacy
artifact:

    overlay_state.py:245   unmigrated = (... + (("newport/",) if facts.newport else ()))
    overlay_state.py:294   "legacy_newport_present", severity="conversion_blocker"
    overlay_state.py:298   invariants.append("dops_with_unmigrated_newport")
    overlay_state.py:299   if not unmigrated: return state="converted"

For a `type port`, a stray `newport/` genuinely is an unfinished migration.
For a `type dport`, `newport/` IS the port, permanently and by design -- the
overlay.dops is a 4-line header with zero ops. So a fully and correctly
migrated dport is indistinguishable from a half-migrated normal port, and
line 299 is unreachable for any of them.

ROOT CAUSE: MISSING INPUT, NOT A WRONG COMPARISON

OverlayFacts (overlay_state.py:35) records only presence:

    overlay_dops: bool = False     # not the declared type
    newport: bool = False

The declared `type` never reaches the assessor, so it cannot distinguish the
two cases even in principle. The planner already extracts it
(engine/planner.py:444-452, TypeDirective -> plan_type).

The same file knows the right answer 200 lines earlier. The bootstrap
decision at overlay_state.py:89-94:

    # A pure dport: newport/ is the whole port -- declare type=dport, drop
    # the now-redundant STATUS (the header carries the type).
    if facts.newport:
        return BootstrapDecision("bootstrap", overlay_type="dport", ...)

So the code can author a dport correctly and then cannot recognise the thing
it authored.

BLAST RADIUS

88 ports in DeltaPorts declare `type dport`, and all 88 have `newport/`
(grep -l '^type dport' ports/*/*/overlay.dops). None can reach `converted`,
so the agent can never auto-fix any of them however correct the fix -- it
will always build green and then escalate with a misleading accusation.

SUGGESTED FIX

1. Carry the declared overlay type into OverlayFacts (parse the `type`
   directive; planner.py already does this).
2. In assess_overlay, exclude `newport/` from `unmigrated` and from the
   `conversion_blocker` rule when the declared type is `dport`.
3. Keep both when the declared type is `port` -- that case is a real
   unfinished migration and the existing guard is right.
4. Consider flagging the inverse (`type dport` with NO newport/) since that
   overlay declares a source tree that does not exist.

The steps.py:1415 gate itself needs no change once the classification is
right.

NOTE ON THE ESCALATION TEXT

Even after the classification is fixed, `patch_non_dops_substrate`'s detail
string asserts a cause ("fix likely written as compat artifacts") it has not
checked. Worth making it name the artifacts it actually found, so a wrong
diagnosis is visible rather than plausible.
title: assess_overlay counts newport/ as unmigrated, so no type-dport port can reach 'converted' and every successful dport patch escalates

description:
In dops-mode compose the compat auto-copy is suppressed
(compose_stages.py:832, `if ctx.mode != "compat": continue`, surfaced as
I_COMPOSE_MODE_DOPS_SUPPRESSES_COMPAT). A file under dragonfly/ therefore
reaches the build ONLY via an explicit `file materialize` op.

Nothing tells the agent when that op is missing. The patch phase cannot
fail on it -- a patch that is not in the composed tree is not applied, and
not applying is not an error -- so the build proceeds and fails for the
original reason. From the agent's side the fix "did not work".

THREE INSTANCES THIS WEEK

1. multimedia/v4l_compat (2026-09-06). Agent wrote the patch, omitted the
   materialize op, and the bundle read as an incomplete fix.

2. www/firefox run 2 (2026-09-07). patch-tools_profiler_lul_LulElfInt.h
   created, not materialized. Caught in review before commit; the composed
   tree had 7 patches where dragonfly/ had 8.

3. www/firefox run 4 (2026-09-08). THE EXPENSIVE ONE.
   patch-config_gcc-stl-wrapper.template.h created, not materialized. The
   agent then spent its last three rounds -- roughly two hours of wall
   clock -- trying variants that landed in the *generated* wrapper headers
   instead, because its correct approach (patch the template that
   generates them) appeared not to work. It never reached a build.

WHAT EXISTS TODAY, AND WHY IT DOES NOT COVER THIS

dportsv3/agent/reconcile.py handles the OPPOSITE direction: when an edit
removes a materialize op and strands its file, reconcile_orphaned_artifacts
deletes the file. Its docstring is explicit that an unreferenced artifact
is "inert ... it does no harm to the build, but it lingers as dead
substrate".

That is true for a stranded file. It is not true for a NEW file: there the
inertness is the whole problem, because the agent believes it applied a fix.

It also runs too late to help. steps.py:1323:

    if (result.status or "").lower() == "success":
        ...
        removed = reconcile_orphaned_artifacts(port_dir)

Success-only, after the attempt, before the diff is captured. A failing
attempt never reaches it, which is exactly the case where the missing op
caused the failure.
design:
Wanted: a signal DURING the attempt, at the moment the agent would
otherwise start a 45-minute build against a tree that does not contain its
change.

Natural home is validate_dops or materialize_dports -- the agent already
calls both, and materialize_dports is the last step before dsynth_build in
practically every round. Either could report:

    dragonfly/ contains 35 files; overlay.dops has 34 `file materialize`
    ops. Unreferenced: patch-config_gcc-stl-wrapper.template.h
    (this file will NOT be applied).

Two design points:

- Warn, do not block. An unreferenced file is legitimate when the agent is
  deliberately retiring a patch -- www/firefox run 5 did exactly that,
  removing the materialize op for a patch it had proved could not work.
  Blocking would have prevented the correct action.

- Distinguish the two directions if cheap. "New file, no op" is nearly
  always a mistake; "op removed, file stranded" is the case reconcile.py
  already cleans up. The wording should not tell the agent to re-add an op
  it deliberately deleted.

The invariant is simply: count(dragonfly/*) == count(`^file materialize`),
and naming the difference is enough. Every instance above would have been
caught by that one line.
title: A dragonfly/ file with no 'file materialize' op is silently inert during the attempt; the agent tests a fix that never reached the build

description:
tool_loop.run appends and never removes. The only mutations of the message
list are:

  tool_loop.py:233   messages.append(_assistant_message_from(response))
  tool_loop.py:293   messages.append(...)

No prune, no cap, no elision anywhere in the file. Context therefore grows
monotonically for the life of an attempt, and since every dsynth_build
outlives the prompt cache, the cost of each build round is whatever the
context has reached by then.

MEASURED (www/firefox, 2026-09-07/08)

  run 4, attempt 1     78k at T1  ->  185k at T106  ->  348k at T124
                       per-eviction cost rose with it, ~140k -> ~348k

  run 3, attempt 1     166k, then one oversized dsynth_log took it to
                       857k, and every later eviction cost ~860k
                       (see poly-9hjm for that call)

Attempts currently get their context reset only by ending. That works --
run 3 attempt 2 restarted at 80,697 after attempt 1 reached 314,527 -- but
it is a reset, not a compaction: everything is re-derived from the bundle,
which is why the first turns of an attempt re-read files the previous
attempt had already read.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE NOW

runner.max_tool_turns is 300 in the live config. A 300-turn attempt on a
big port does ~15 build rounds; with unbounded growth the last rounds cost
several times the first. The turn cap is only usable if the per-turn cost
does not climb with turn number.
design:
THE POLICY IS ALREADY WRITTEN

fix_chat.render_session_transcript (fix_chat.py:101) does exactly the
right thing, and its docstring states the reasoning:

    "When over cap, keeps the head and tail and elides the middle: the
     head holds the failure + triage + first-move reasoning, the tail
     holds the winning approach + rebuild proof -- both are what 'why'
     questions hinge on. The repeated middle build cycles are the most
     expendable. Whole-block, so no turn is cut mid-sentence (a single
     oversized block is head+tail clipped first)."

DEFAULT_CONTEXT_CAP = 96 * 1024 (fix_chat.py:31).

It is only reached from the tracker's fix-review chat --
agentic_api.py:373 via build_chat_messages -- which is a tools-off Q&A
over frozen artifacts. The loop that actually accumulates context never
uses it.

"The repeated middle build cycles are the most expendable" describes a
300-turn porting attempt more accurately than it describes the review
chat.

WHY THIS IS CHEAP

fix_chat's elision is pure text/block manipulation. It costs nothing to
run. Claude-Code-style compaction by summarisation would cost one full
context read to apply -- at 860k that is a 17% tax just to shrink.

CARE NEEDED

- fix_chat renders tool_calls as text because it runs tools-off. A live
  loop must keep the structured tool_call/tool_result pairing intact, so
  elision has to drop whole call+result pairs, not rewrite them.
- Dropping a tool result the model still refers to will confuse it. The
  head/tail shape helps (recent turns survive) but the boundary needs
  thought.
- Interacts with worker's "you already have this" dedup
  (reset_attempt_caches, worker.py:1352): if an elided file read is later
  deduped as already-seen, the model is refused content it no longer has.
  That failure mode is already documented in attempt_loop.py:399.

REVISED 2026-09-16: mask old tool output, don't drop exchanges.

1294712 (unpushed) did the first design: over a byte cap, leave the oldest
whole exchanges out of the request. The literature says that is the variant
nobody uses: it deletes the agent's actions and its failed turns.

WHAT THE EVIDENCE SAYS

- JetBrains, "The Complexity Trap" (arXiv 2508.21433, NeurIPS'25 DL4Code).
  SWE-agent and OpenHands on SWE-bench Verified, five model setups.
  Replacing tool observations older than the last 10 turns with a
  placeholder, while keeping every reasoning step and action, cut cost
  by more than half and matched or beat LLM summarization in 4 of 5
  settings (Qwen3-Coder: +2.6 points solved, 52% cheaper). Summarization
  made agents run 15% longer, cost up to 7% on its own, and got almost no
  cache reuse. The window is agent-specific and must be tuned.
- Anthropic clear_tool_uses_20250919: keep the calls, replace old results
  with a placeholder, keep=3 by default, exclude_tools, and clear_at_least
  so each cache invalidation is worth paying for. Clearing +29%, clearing
  plus the memory tool +39% on their agentic-search eval.
- Manus: prompt-cache hit rate is the top cost metric; append-only
  context; restorable compression (drop content, keep the path); keep
  failed turns visible.
- Server-side context editing and compaction are out of reach: the
  harness calls chat.completions / litellm on OpenAI-compatible endpoints.

GAP SPECIFIC TO THIS HARNESS

Masking relies on the model's reasoning surviving it. In misc/py-onnx
(2026-09-16) 0 of 138 assistant turns stored reasoning_content and 19 had
any text, so masked outputs would take the why with them. The literature's
answer is note-taking (Anthropic's memory tool, Manus's todo.md).

CONSIDERED AND REJECTED

Masking when a slow tool call has probably let the cache expire, to make
the mask free. Measured on py-onnx: 60-120s calls preceded a miss 2 times
in 10, and 5 misses followed no long call at all. Not predictable enough.

DESIGN

1. tool_loop masks tool results older than llm.patch.context_keep_turns
   (default 10) with a fixed placeholder that keeps ok/rebuild_ok and says
   to repeat the call. Calls are never masked. messages, and so the
   session dump, keep everything; only the request is masked.
2. Batched: mask once llm.patch.context_mask_batch bytes (32KB) of old
   output are maskable, so the cached prefix holds between masks.
3. dops_reference and note are never masked. A mask resets get_file's
   scroll-back dedup.
4. note(text): the agent records why a build failed. Calls are never
   masked, and the retry hand-over carries the notes to the next attempt.
5. No LLM summarization until a measured need.

MEASURE: observations_masked (count, bytes, turn), repeat_after_mask (a
read repeated after its output was masked), turns per attempt, cost,
rebuild_ok rate.
REVIEWED 2026-09-16 (still uncommitted, on top of 1294712)

• Placeholders said "Repeat the call" for every tool. Repeating dsynth_build rebuilds; repeating edit_file applies the edit twice. Only reads say it now; dsynth_build points at dsynth_log, edit_file/put_file at get_file.
• Results under 512 bytes are not masked. On py-onnx they were 46 of 160 results and 4% of the bytes: validate_dops diagnostics, refused writes, edit confirmations. Masking them saved 2%.
• An empty note is refused. The hand-over carries at most 20 notes, 500 chars each. runner.log shows the note text.
